newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE drifts lower, quiet ahead of U.S. FOMC.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE drifts lower, quiet ahead of U.S. FOMC.

text.p: UK shares were mostly lower in late Tuesday morning trade, albeit in thin volume as investors preferred to sit tight awaiting the FOMC's decision on whether to raise U.S. interest rates.
The leading FTSE 100 index was down 15.4 points at 4,629.8 by 1007 GMT, near the bottom of the day's 20-point trading range. Declining stocks outnumbered climbers two and a half times.
"The market looks set to continue drifting off," said one dealer. "But there's no real selling pressure, its just nerves ahead of the FOMC."
Trading volume was a meagre 181 million shares.

The Federal Reserve policymakers meet on Tuesday to consider raising interest rates for the second time in three months. A Reuters poll of 39 U.S. primary dealers on Monday showed 21 expected no change in rates while 18 believed the federal funds rate would be raised to 5.75 percent from 5.5.

In the meantime, uncertainty over the decision was dampening sentiment. "The market looks to be nervous ahead of the rate decision," said Steve Wright, UK equity strategist at BZW who expects to see a 25 basis point rate increase. "It is concerned that it could take quite a lot of tightening to slow growth down and is wondering how many rate rises we are going to see."
Dealers agreed that whether there was a rate rise or not, Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks about inflation would be carefully scrutinized.

"Ultimately, if we do get an increase, then part of the market is bound to be surprised," said one senior equity salesman. "But what is important is the overtone in Greenspan's statement..." he said. "We want to know how he is reading inflation, and that will help people decide what to do."
Earlier, London stocks had got off to a steady start, the FTSE 100 rose to 4,646.2 at its best, but the positive influence from a firmer performance in New York soon ran out.
The Dow managed to finish with a 34 point gain on Monday following a sharp 139 point setback on Friday.
UK gilt futures meanwhile stayed firm, buoyed by a successful auction of 1.5 billion stg of 2002 gilts, which attracted cover of 3.03 times and was sold without a yield or price tail.

Among stock features, shares in retailer Marks & Spencer Plc fell 5-1/2p to 503-1/2 after the company reported annual profits of 1.102 billion stg, towards the lower end of analysts expectations. The company added that if the strong pound stays at current levels, it could cut 1997/8 profits by 20 million stg.

Shares in composite insurer, Royal & Sun Alliance also fell 10-1/2p to 479 after the group announced operating pre-tax profits of 195 million stg, at the top end of analysts forecasts. The company also confirmed plans to buy back five percent of its own share capital.

Elsewhere, Dixons shed 12p to 484p after a press report said the Office of Fair Trading could launch an inquiry into alleged anti-competitive tactics to exclude rivals from out-of-town shopping centres. Dixons said later it had made its position clear to the OFT and said it had "absolutely no market power" in new retail parks.
